content:
Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg fired back on Monday after President Donald Trump claimed he “ruined the system” that caused Friday’s nationwide flight shutdown, noting on X, “As secretary, I made sure to leave air travel in better condition than when we arrived.”

“We reversed a decade of decline in air traffic controller staffing, drove down runway safety incidents, and when I left office we were experiencing the lowest flight cancellation rates in years,” wrote Buttigieg, who held the job under ex-President Joe Biden from 2021 to 2025.

The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday that halted all activity in U.S. airspace for more than four hours, which Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed on outdated equipment he demanded $50 billion in taxpayer dollars to fix.

Vice President JD Vance claimed Monday that Democrats in Congress have been too focused on “men in women’s sports” to help address the issue, and Trump falsely told reporters, “And Buttigieg ruined the system, he totally ruined it.”

While the Trump administration blamed old equipment for the fiasco, which affected 1.5 million passengers on some 11,000 flights, Buttigieg noted that he “launched a project to transition the FAA’s communication systems from copper wire to a modern network.”

“I am glad the Trump administration has continued that work, but they have so far failed to explain why their execution of it triggered the worst FAA communications breakdown this century,” Buttigieg wrote Monday in his reaction to a clip of Trump blaming him.

Buttigieg’s Department of Transportation described how the Biden administration was transitioning from copper wires to fiber-optic cables and wireless systems to improve the FAA’s “navigation, surveillance, and communications systems.”

“I support more funding for FAA upgrades, but this episode is another blow to the public’s confidence that the administration can deliver,” Buttigieg wrote Monday.

The groundstop on Friday left Americans worried about potential cyberattacks from foreign adversaries amid Trump’s ongoing war on Iran, and came one day after a global Microsoft outage that left millions without email and other services.

Congress passed legislation last year that allocates $4.75 billion for “telecommunications infrastructure modernization and systems upgrades.”

While Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday that old equipment was to blame for the shutdown and that there was “zero evidence” of a cyberattack, Buttigieg demanded more details on Monday.

He wrote, “The Trump administration owes Americans an honest accounting of how they have spent the billions of dollars already authorized, clearer answers on why their repair work brought down the entire system on Friday, and an explanation of what they are doing.”
